claims.text: Kawasaki dz = diagnosed clinically: fever for ≥ 5 days plus 4 of the 5 criteria.
claims.quote: Diagnosis is made if fever ≥ 38.0° C (about 100.4° F) has occurred for ≥ 5 days and 4 of the following 5 criteria are noted:
claims.locator: Table: Criteria for Diagnosis of Kawasaki Disease

claims.text: Kawasaki dz: serial ECG and echocardiography.
Labs to r/o mimics of Kawasaki dz: CBC, ESR, CRP, albumin, liver enzymes, throat and blood cx, UA and CXR.
claims.quote: Testing to rule out other disorders: complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, albumin, liver enzymes, throat and blood cultures, urinalysis, chest radiograph

claims.text: Scarlet fever (group A strep): a (+) rapid Ag test confirms it; confirm a (−) one w throat cx in children.
claims.quote: Thus, positive results can establish the diagnosis, but negative results, at least in children, should be confirmed by culture.

claims.text: ASO and anti-DNase B titers help w post-streptococcal comp such as rheumatic fever, ⍉w the acute infect.
claims.quote: Antistreptococcal antibody tests are not useful in diagnosing acute GABHS infection because antibodies first develop several weeks after GABHS infection begins and a single high antibody titer is more likely to reflect an infection that occurred in the distant past. Antibodies are most useful in diagnosis of poststreptococcal sequelae, such as rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. Antistreptolysin O (ASO) and antideoxyribonuclease B (anti-DNase B) titers begin to increase about 1 week after the GABHS infection and peak about 1 to 2 months after the infection.
